intro.why: Every later module is one cell of this taxonomy. Knowing which cell a problem lives in tells you the data you need, the loss you optimise and how you evaluate.

sections.title: AI vs data science vs machine learning
sections.plain: ML sits inside AI and is a tool of data science.
sections.body:
• Artificial intelligence: technology for machines to understand, interpret, learn and make "intelligent" decisions. It includes ML among other fields (search, planning, logic).
  • Machine learning: algorithms that help machines improve through supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. A subset of AI and a tool of data science.
  • Data science: collection, preparation and analysis of data, using AI/ML, research, industry expertise and statistics to make business decisions.

The slides' Venn diagram: ML ⊂ AI, and data science overlaps both.

sections.title: Definitions of machine learning
sections.plain: Learning = performance on a task improves with experience.
sections.body:
• "The science (and art) of programming computers so they can learn from data."
  • General: "Field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed" (Samuel).
  • Engineering (Mitchell): an algorithm learns if it improves its performance P at some task T with experience E. A well-defined learning task is the triple $\langle P,T,E\rangle$.

Traditional programming: Data + Program → Computer → Output. ML: Data + Output → Computer → Program (p.11).

ExampleTPE
1Recognise handwritten words% words correctly classifiedHuman-labelled images
2Spam vs legitimate email% emails correctly classifiedEmails with human labels
3Play checkers% games wonGames played against itself
4Drive on 4-lane highways with visionAverage distance before an errorImages + steering commands from a human driver

sections.title: Traditional vs ML approach: spam filtering
sections.plain: Hand-written rules grow unmaintainable; learned rules adapt.
sections.body:
Traditional: study the problem → write rules (e.g. "4U", "credit card", "free", "amazing") → evaluate → analyse errors → write more rules. Challenge: a long list of complex rules that is hard to maintain.

ML: study the problem → train an ML algorithm on data → evaluate → analyse errors → launch. The algorithm learns which phrases predict spam by detecting unusually frequent words in spam vs "ham". The program is shorter, easier to maintain and usually more accurate, and retraining on updated data can be automated (p.16).

sections.title: Application perspectives
sections.plain: Prediction, sequences, planning and problem solving.
sections.body:
• Object categorisation / prediction: medical diagnosis, transaction analysis, recommendations, speech-to-text.
  • Sequence: forecasting, medical research, recommendation, content management.
  • Planning: navigation, path finding, gaming, control.
  • Problem solving: pattern recognition, optimisation, decision systems.

sections.title: When to use machine learning
sections.plain: Use ML when rules are unknown, unexplainable, personal or changing.
sections.body:
ML is used when (p.20):

  • human expertise does not exist (navigating on Mars);
  • humans can't explain their expertise (biometrics, speech);
  • models must be customised (personalised medicine);
  • Beyond the slides the environment changes (spam, fraud).

Learning isn't always useful: there is no need to "learn" to calculate payroll. Pattern recognition (p.21, handwritten digits) illustrates the case where rules can't be articulated: the variety of ways to write a "2" defeats hand-coding.

sections.plain: Feedback, no feedback, or delayed rewards.
sections.body:

FeedbackYes (labels)NoneDelayed reward/penalty
Data$\{(x_i,y_i)\}$$\{x_i\}$Interaction $(s_t,a_t,r_t)$
ProblemsRegression, classificationClustering, associationReward-based control
ApproachMap labelled inputs to known outputsDiscover patternsTrial and error

Features (attributes, predictors) describe each example. Slide examples: employability prediction from CGPA, communication, aptitude and programming skills (label: job offered?); used-car price from brand, year, engine capacity, mileage, distance travelled, cab? (label: price); market segmentation from income, visits, spend, zip code (no label; find 2, 3, 4… groups).

sections.title: Supervised learning: classification and regression
sections.plain: Learn f from labelled pairs; y categorical or real-valued.
sections.body:
Given $(x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_n,y_n)$, learn $f(x)$ to predict $y$ for previously unseen $x$.

  • Classification: $y$ categorical. Goal: assign a class to unseen records as accurately as possible. Example: tumour size → benign (0) / malignant (1) with the learned rule "if $x>T$ malignant else benign" (p.28). With more features (age, clump thickness, cell size/shape uniformity) the boundary becomes a line or hyperplane.
  • Regression: $y$ real-valued, e.g. September Arctic sea-ice extent by year (p.33), fitted with a line or a curve.

Workflow (p.32): training images + labels → features → training → learned model; test image → features → learned model → prediction.

Techniques (p.31): linear and logistic regression, naïve Bayes, SVMs, decision trees and random forests, neural networks. Applications: image classification, face recognition, spam filters, document tagging, fraud detection.

Beyond the slides Formally we pick $h\in\mathcal H$ minimising empirical risk $\hat R(h)=\frac1n\sum_i\ell(h(x_i),y_i)$, hoping it also has low true risk $R(h)=\mathbb E_{(x,y)}[\ell(h(x),y)]$. The gap between the two is the generalisation error, which is why we evaluate on a held-out test set.

sections.title: Unsupervised learning
sections.body:
Given $x_1,\dots,x_n$ without labels, output hidden structure. Clustering goal: minimise intra-cluster distances and maximise inter-cluster distances.

  • Applications: recommendation, targeted marketing, spam filters, news grouping, campaigning.
  • Clustering: k-means, hierarchical clustering, expectation maximisation (ML Module 10).
  • Visualisation / dimensionality reduction: PCA, kernel PCA, LLE, t-SNE.

Unsupervised learning can also have a test phase: assign a new cat/dog image to the cluster with the closer centroid (p.37).

sections.title: Reinforcement learning and the full taxonomy
sections.plain: Observe, act, get reward, update policy, repeat.
sections.body:
Loop (p.38): 1 observe, 2 select action using policy, 3 act, 4 get reward or penalty, 5 update policy, 6 iterate until an optimal policy is found. Beyond the slides The objective is to maximise expected discounted return $\mathbb E\left[\sum_t\gamma^t r_t\right]$ with $0\le\gamma<1$.

Taxonomy (p.39): supervised (continuous target → regression, e.g. house prices; categorical → classification, e.g. medical imaging); unsupervised (clustering → customer segmentation; association → market basket); semi-supervised (classification → text; clustering → lane finding); reinforcement (classification → optimised marketing; control → driverless cars).

sections.title: Semi-supervised learning
sections.plain: A few labels plus many unlabelled points.
sections.body: Partially labelled data: some labelled, a lot unlabelled. Combines unsupervised and supervised algorithms (e.g. cluster first, then label clusters from the few labelled points). Example: photo-hosting services (Google Photos) that group faces, then need only one name per person.

sections.title: Batch, mini-batch and online learning
sections.plain: All data at once, chunks, or one example at a time.
sections.body:
• Batch: uses all available data at a time during training.
  • Mini-batch: a subset at a time.
  • Online (incremental): a single instance at a time; new data arriving on the fly keeps updating the model, and huge datasets can be chopped into pieces (out-of-core learning).

Beyond the slides An online update has the form $\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\eta\nabla\ell(h_{\theta_t}(x_t),y_t)$; the learning rate $\eta$ controls how fast the model forgets old data.

sections.title: Instance-based vs model-based learning
sections.plain: Compare to stored examples vs fit a model.
sections.body:
• Instance-based: compare new data points to known data points (e.g. k-nearest neighbours, ML Module 6). No explicit training; cost moves to prediction time.
  • Model-based: detect patterns in the training data and build a predictive model (e.g. a decision boundary); training data can then be discarded.

Trade-off chart (p.47, labelled "unscientific & opinionated"): lasso and linear/logistic regression are highly interpretable but less accurate; decision trees and naïve Bayes are in the middle; random forests, boosting, SVMs, neural nets and deep learning are most accurate on real-world data but least interpretable. See ML Module 11 for interpretability.

sections.title: The ML workflow and the car-price case study
sections.plain: From 'should I use ML?' to evaluating on a test set.
sections.body:
1. Should I use ML? Is there a pattern? Can I solve it analytically? Do I have data?
  2. Gather and organise data.
  3. Preprocess, clean, visualise.
  4. Choose a model, loss, regularisation.
  5. Optimise.
  6. Hyperparameter search.
  7. Analyse performance and mistakes; iterate to step 5 (or 3).

Demo case study (p.50): car price from mileage. Steps: define the objective; gather data (survey, past purchases); preprocess (train/test split, input representation); explore; choose a model (linear regression); objective function; optimisation; evaluate on the test set (generalisation).

sections.title: The learning problem, formally
sections.plain: Minimise average loss on data; hope it generalises.
sections.body:
Assume examples are drawn i.i.d. from an unknown distribution $p(x,y)$. We choose a hypothesis class $\mathcal H$ and a loss $\ell$, then solve

$$\hat h=\arg\min_{h\in\mathcal H}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(h(x_i),y_i)\ (+\lambda\,\Omega(h)).$$

Common losses: squared error (regression), 0–1 or cross-entropy (classification). The regulariser $\Omega$ limits complexity. Inductive bias is everything that makes us prefer some $h$ over others (the choice of $\mathcal H$, $\Omega$, the optimiser).

Assumptions and limitations: i.i.d. data (violated by drift and time series), representative training data, labels that are correct; ML finds correlations, not causes.

sections.title: Common technical misconceptions
sections.body:
• "High training accuracy means a good model." Only test-set performance estimates generalisation.
  • "Unsupervised means no evaluation." Use silhouette scores, stability, or downstream task performance.
  • "Online learning is just faster batch learning." It changes behaviour: recent data dominates, which helps with drift but can forget.
  • "Instance-based methods don't learn." They defer generalisation to query time; choosing $k$ and the distance is still learning.
  • "Correlation found by ML is causal." Interventions need causal analysis.

code.title: Supervised vs unsupervised on the same data
code.explain: Fits a classifier with the labels, then clusters the same points without labels, and compares.
mistakes: Expecting cluster numbers to match class numbers.
code.notes: Adjusted Rand index compares a clustering with known labels when they exist.
code.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, adjusted_rand_score

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)                      # 150 flowers, 4 features, 3 species

# Supervised: learn from labelled examples, evaluate on unseen ones
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=y)
clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("supervised test accuracy:", round(accuracy_score(y_te, clf.predict(X_te)), 3))

# Unsupervised: same features, no labels; find 3 groups
km = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X)
print("cluster sizes:", sorted(int((km.labels_ == k).sum()) for k in range(3)))
print("agreement with true species (ARI):", round(adjusted_rand_score(y, km.labels_), 3))
code.output:
supervised test accuracy: 0.956
cluster sizes: [38, 50, 62]
agreement with true species (ARI): 0.73

code.title: Constant baseline vs linear model on the slides' car data
code.explain: Reproduces the demo case study: L1 error of H0 = 9, the best constant (median), and a least-squares line.
mistakes: Skipping the baseline: always know what 'predict a constant' scores.
code.notes: With four points this is illustrative only; real work needs a held-out test set.
code.code:
import numpy as np

mileage = np.array([9.8, 9.12, 9.5, 10.0])      # kmpl  (slides p.50)
price   = np.array([10.48, 1.75, 6.95, 2.51])   # crore

H0 = 9.0
print("L1 errors for H0 = 9:", np.abs(price - H0).round(2), "total", round(np.abs(price - H0).sum(), 2))

best_c = np.median(price)                        # minimises total absolute error
print("best constant (median):", round(best_c, 2), "total L1", round(np.abs(price - best_c).sum(), 2))

slope, intercept = np.polyfit(mileage, price, 1) # least-squares line
pred = intercept + slope * mileage
print(f"line: price = {intercept:.2f} + {slope:.2f} * mileage, total L1 {np.abs(price - pred).sum():.2f}")
code.output:
L1 errors for H0 = 9: [1.48 7.25 2.05 6.49] total 17.27
best constant (median): 4.73 total L1 13.17
line: price = -26.35 + 3.31 * mileage, total L1 12.57
